featuredImage.alt: How Property Managers Can Streamline Eviction Cleanouts

c: An eviction can create a long list of tasks for a property manager.

Once a tenant has legally vacated a rental unit, the property may need to be inspected, cleaned, repaired, and prepared for the next occupant. In some cases, there may also be furniture, mattresses, appliances, boxes, garbage, and other belongings left behind.
This is where an
becomes important.

For property managers, the goal is not simply to remove everything from a unit. A well-organized cleanout process can help reduce delays, coordinate contractors, restore the property, and get the rental ready for its next stage as efficiently as possible.

, we provide professional junk removal and property cleanout services throughout Toronto and the GTA, helping property managers handle the physical removal of unwanted items from rental properties.

blocks.text: What Is an Eviction Cleanout?

c: An
eviction cleanout
involves removing unwanted belongings, furniture, appliances, garbage, and other materials left inside a rental property after a tenant has vacated.
Depending on the property, an eviction cleanout may include:

items: Removal of damaged or unwanted items
Preparation of the property for cleaning and repairs

c: Every eviction is different. Some units may only need a few items removed, while others may require a complete property cleanout.

blocks.text: First: Make Sure the Property Is Legally Ready for Cleanout

c: Before scheduling an eviction cleanout, property managers should confirm that they have the legal authority to remove and dispose of the tenant’s belongings.
In Ontario, landlords must follow the

when dealing with tenant property. For example, when an eviction order has been enforced, the landlord generally cannot sell, retain, or otherwise dispose of the tenant’s property until 72 hours have passed. The tenant’s belongings must also be made available for retrieval during the applicable period.

Different rules can apply when a tenant has abandoned a rental unit. Ontario’s legislation sets out specific requirements for disposing of property in an abandoned unit, including notice and waiting-period requirements for certain belongings.

b: Property managers should confirm the applicable requirements before authorizing disposal.

c: Once the property is legally ready, the physical cleanout can be planned.

blocks.text: 1. Inspect the Property Before Booking the Cleanout

c: One of the easiest ways to streamline an eviction cleanout is to inspect the unit before the removal crew arrives.
Create a basic inventory of what needs to be removed.
Look at:
Take photos if appropriate for your property-management records.
This gives you a better understanding of the amount of material involved and helps the junk removal company prepare for the job.

blocks.text: 2. Separate Items That Should Not Be Removed

c: Not everything inside an evicted property should automatically go into the junk pile.
Before the cleanout, identify:

items: Appliances that are part of the rental
Items subject to a tenant’s retrieval rights

c: This step can prevent accidental removal of something that should remain at the property or be handled separately.

blocks.text: 3. Create a Room-by-Room Cleanout Plan

c: Instead of approaching the entire property as one large job, break it into sections.
For example:
mattress, bed frame, dresser and boxes
furniture and household items
sofa, chairs, table and miscellaneous items
unwanted appliances and loose items
boxes, furniture and general junk
A room-by-room approach makes it easier to estimate the volume of junk and determine what needs to be removed first.

blocks.text: 4. Book Junk Removal as Early as Possible

c: If the property needs to be cleaned, repaired, painted, photographed, or listed again, delays in junk removal can affect the entire schedule.
Once the property is legally ready and the scope of the cleanout is known, schedule the removal service as early as practical.
This is particularly important when:

items: A new tenant is waiting to move in
The landlord wants to list the property
Multiple units are being turned over

c: Coordinating junk removal early can help prevent contractors from waiting for an empty property.

blocks.text: 5. Tell the Removal Company What Is Inside the Property

c: Give the junk removal company as much information as possible before the appointment.
Mention if the property contains:
Photos can also be useful when requesting a quote.
The more accurate the information, the easier it is to plan the appropriate crew, vehicle, and equipment.

blocks.text: 6. Consider the Access Before the Crew Arrives

c: Access can significantly affect how quickly an eviction cleanout can be completed.
Check:
For apartment buildings and condos, property managers should also confirm whether the building requires advance notice for movers or junk removal crews.
Having these details ready can prevent unnecessary delays on cleanout day.

blocks.text: 7. Remove Large Furniture First

c: Large furniture can take up a significant amount of space inside a property.
Items may include:
Removing large pieces first can make the remaining items easier to access.
It can also create more working space for the crew as the cleanout progresses.

blocks.text: 8. Handle Appliances Separately

c: Eviction cleanouts may also involve unwanted appliances such as:
Some appliances require specific handling or recycling processes.
Property managers should identify appliances in advance rather than treating them as ordinary household junk.
Where practical, responsible disposal and recycling can help keep reusable materials and recyclable components out of the landfill.

blocks.text: 9. Prioritize Safety

c: An eviction property isn’t always left in perfect condition.
The unit may contain:
Property managers should communicate known safety concerns before the crew arrives.
A junk removal company can handle ordinary unwanted household items, but

b: hazardous materials, biohazards, serious mould contamination, and certain specialized materials may require a qualified specialist

c: Do not ask a general junk removal crew to handle materials outside the company’s accepted scope.

blocks.text: 10. Coordinate Cleanout With Repairs and Cleaning

c: An eviction cleanout is usually only one step in preparing a rental property.
A typical turnover may look something like:

b: Eviction completed → property legally ready → belongings removed → repairs → deep cleaning → inspection → listing or new tenant

c: Removing junk before repairs and deep cleaning usually makes the rest of the work easier.
For example, a contractor cannot properly repair a damaged wall if furniture and boxes are blocking access.
Similarly, cleaners can work more efficiently when floors, counters, closets, and rooms are accessible.

blocks.text: 11. Don’t Forget Basements, Garages and Storage Areas

c: Property managers sometimes focus on the main living area and overlook additional spaces.
During the inspection, check:
Tenants may leave belongings in these areas even when the main unit appears relatively empty.
Including these spaces in the original cleanout plan can prevent the need for a second removal appointment.

blocks.text: 12. Keep a Clear Record of the Cleanout

c: Property managers often handle multiple units and multiple turnovers at the same time.
Keeping basic records can make the process easier.
Consider documenting:

items: Any items that were preserved or separately handled

c: Good documentation can also make communication easier between landlords, property managers, contractors, and vendors.

blocks.text: 13. Use One Reliable Junk Removal Company for Multiple Properties

c: Property managers who regularly deal with tenant turnovers may benefit from having a reliable junk removal provider they can contact when a unit needs clearing.
Instead of finding a new company for every eviction, having an established process can save time.
A property manager can keep the provider’s contact information available and provide the same basic details for each job:
This makes recurring property cleanouts easier to coordinate.

blocks.text: Final Thoughts

c: An eviction cleanout doesn’t have to become another source of stress for property managers.
The key is to create a clear process:

b: Confirm the property is legally ready → inspect the unit → identify what needs to be removed → schedule junk removal → clear the property → arrange repairs and cleaning → prepare for the next tenant.

c: By planning the cleanout early, communicating clearly with the removal company, and coordinating the work with contractors, property managers can make rental turnovers more organized and efficient.
Most importantly, remember that

b: tenant belongings should not be disposed of simply because a tenant has been evicted

c: . Ontario’s rules contain specific requirements concerning the handling and disposal of tenant property, so property managers should confirm that the applicable legal steps and timelines have been followed before authorizing disposal.
